title: Rates of Reaction
description: How to measure and change reaction rates — collision theory, factors affecting rate, catalysts, and interpreting rate graphs.

notes.heading: Collision Theory
notes.body: For a chemical reaction to occur, reactant particles must: (1) Collide with each other. (2) Collide with sufficient energy (the activation energy). (3) Collide with the correct orientation. Only successful collisions lead to a reaction. Collision theory explains why reaction rates vary: increasing the frequency of successful collisions increases the rate. Activation energy is the minimum energy needed to break bonds in the reactants and start the reaction. Even exothermic reactions require activation energy (e.g., a spark to ignite methane, even though burning is highly exothermic). Think of it like pushing a boulder over a hill — it takes energy to get it over the top, even though it will roll down with great force afterwards.

illustration.alt: Diagram comparing an unsuccessful particle collision with a successful collision that forms a product.
illustration.caption: A reaction only occurs when particles collide with enough energy and the correct orientation.

notes.heading: Factors Affecting Reaction Rate
notes.body: Four main factors increase reaction rate by increasing collision frequency or the proportion of successful collisions: (1) Temperature — higher temperature = particles have more kinetic energy → move faster → collide more often AND with more energy → a higher proportion of collisions exceed the activation energy → faster rate. A 10°C rise typically doubles the rate. (2) Concentration (solutions) / Pressure (gases) — more particles per unit volume → more frequent collisions → faster rate. (3) Surface area (solids) — smaller pieces (powder vs large lumps) → greater surface area exposed → more particles available to collide → faster rate. (4) Catalysts — substances that increase reaction rate without being used up. They provide an alternative reaction pathway with LOWER activation energy, so a higher proportion of collisions are successful. Catalysts are NOT consumed — they can be reused. Enzymes are biological catalysts.

illustration.alt: Four panels showing how temperature, concentration, surface area and catalysts affect reaction rate.
illustration.caption: Higher temperature, concentration, surface area and catalysts all increase the rate by increasing successful collisions.

notes.heading: Measuring Reaction Rates
notes.body: Rate of reaction = amount of reactant used OR product formed ÷ time. Common methods: (1) Measuring gas volume — collect gas in a gas syringe or inverted measuring cylinder; measure volume at regular intervals. (2) Measuring mass loss — if a gas is produced and escapes, the mass decreases; place the reaction on a balance. (3) Colour change/turbidity — time how long it takes for a cross to disappear under a reaction flask (sodium thiosulfate + HCl → sulfur precipitate forms, obscuring cross). (4) pH change — monitor pH with a probe (for reactions producing/consuming H⁺). (5) Temperature change — measure temperature rise/fall over time. The rate changes DURING a reaction — it is fastest at the start (highest concentration of reactants) and slows as reactants are used up. The average rate is total change ÷ total time. The instantaneous rate at a specific time is the gradient of the tangent to the curve at that point.

illustration.alt: Four common methods for measuring reaction rate: gas volume, mass loss, turbidity and pH or temperature change.
illustration.caption: Rate can be measured as gas volume, mass loss, cross disappearance, or pH/temperature change over time.

notes.heading: Interpreting Rate Graphs
notes.body: Graphs of amount of product vs time show characteristic shapes: the curve rises steeply initially (fastest rate — highest reactant concentration), then gradually levels off to a plateau (reaction complete — limiting reactant used up). The steeper the initial gradient, the faster the reaction. Comparing graphs: higher temperature/concentration/surface area → steeper initial gradient → faster rate → reaches the same final amount but in less time. The plateau height is the same if the same amount of reactants is used — the final amount of product is determined by the limiting reactant, not the rate. Graphs of mass loss vs time slope downwards (mass decreases as gas escapes) and plateau when reaction is complete. To calculate rate from a graph: (1) Average rate = change in y ÷ change in x over the whole reaction. (2) Rate at a specific time = draw a tangent at that time, calculate its gradient.

illustration.alt: Product-versus-time graph showing a steep initial rate, a plateau and a tangent for instantaneous rate.
illustration.caption: The initial gradient is fastest; the plateau means the limiting reactant is used up.

notes.heading: Catalysts in Detail
notes.body: A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with lower activation energy. On an energy profile diagram, a catalysed reaction has a lower 'hump' (activation energy) but the same energy difference between reactants and products (ΔH is unchanged). Catalysts do NOT affect: the equilibrium position, the amount of product formed, or whether a reaction is endo/exothermic. They only affect the RATE. Industrial importance: many industrial processes use catalysts to run at lower temperatures and pressures, saving energy and money. Examples: Iron in the Haber process (N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ — making ammonia for fertilisers). Vanadium(V) oxide in the Contact process (SO₂ → SO₃ — making sulfuric acid). Platinum/palladium in catalytic converters (convert toxic CO and NOₓ into CO₂ and N₂). Nickel in hydrogenation of vegetable oils (making margarine). Biological catalysts (enzymes): highly specific, work at optimum temperature and pH. Catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂ → H₂O + O₂) — this can be demonstrated with liver or potato tissue.

illustration.alt: Energy profile comparing catalysed and uncatalysed reactions.
illustration.caption: A catalyst lowers the activation energy but does not change ΔH or the final amount of product.

notes.heading: Practical: Investigating Rate Factors
notes.body: Classic rate experiments: (1) Effect of concentration on rate — magnesium ribbon + hydrochloric acid at different concentrations. Measure volume of H₂ gas produced over time. Controlled variables: mass/length of Mg ribbon, volume of acid, temperature. Expectation: higher [HCl] → steeper initial gradient → faster reaction. (2) Effect of surface area — marble chips (CaCO₃) vs powdered CaCO₃ + HCl. Measure mass loss (CO₂ escapes) or gas volume. Powder reacts faster (greater surface area). (3) Effect of temperature — sodium thiosulfate + HCl at different temperatures. Time how long for a cross drawn on paper to disappear (sulfur precipitate). Expectation: higher temperature → faster disappearance. (4) Catalysis — decomposition of H₂O₂ with manganese(IV) oxide (MnO₂) catalyst vs no catalyst. The catalyst dramatically speeds up oxygen production. Collect O₂ gas over time to measure rate.

illustration.alt: Four practical setups for investigating concentration, surface area, temperature and catalysis effects.
illustration.caption: Classic experiments include Mg + HCl, marble chips vs powder, thiosulfate cross and H₂O₂ with MnO₂.

notes.heading: Explaining Rate Changes (Maxwell-Boltzmann)
notes.body: At a given temperature, not all particles have the same kinetic energy — there is a distribution of energies (Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution). Only particles with energy ≥ activation energy can react. Increasing temperature: (1) Shifts the distribution to higher energies. (2) A much larger proportion of particles now exceed the activation energy. (3) Particles also collide more frequently. This is why a small temperature increase can cause a large rate increase — the number of particles with sufficient energy increases exponentially, not linearly. A catalyst works by lowering the activation energy barrier — on the distribution curve, this means a larger proportion of particles can now react without changing the temperature. This is why catalysts are so effective — they enable previously 'inactive' particles to participate in reactions.

illustration.alt: Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curves at two temperatures with an activation energy line.
illustration.caption: Raising temperature shifts the distribution right, so more particles have enough energy to react.

flashcards.definition: Reactions occur when particles collide with sufficient energy (≥ activation energy) AND correct orientation.
flashcards.example: Not every collision causes a reaction — only successful ones do.

flashcards.definition: Minimum energy required for a reaction to occur — energy to break bonds in reactants. Even exothermic reactions need it.
flashcards.example: Methane + oxygen is exothermic but needs a spark (activation energy) to start.

flashcards.definition: A substance that increases reaction rate by providing an alternative pathway with lower activation energy. NOT consumed in the reaction.
flashcards.example: MnO₂ catalyses H₂O₂ decomposition. Enzymes are biological catalysts.

flashcards.definition: Higher temperature → particles move faster → more frequent collisions with more energy → higher proportion exceed activation energy → faster rate.
flashcards.example: A 10°C rise typically doubles the reaction rate.

flashcards.definition: Higher concentration → more particles per unit volume → more frequent collisions → faster rate.
flashcards.example: Mg reacts faster with 2M HCl than with 0.5M HCl.

flashcards.term: Effect of surface area on rate
flashcards.definition: Smaller pieces (powder) → greater surface area exposed → more particles available for collision → faster rate.
flashcards.example: Powdered CaCO₃ reacts faster with acid than large marble chips.

flashcards.definition: Amount of reactant used or product formed ÷ time. Units: g/s, cm³/s, mol/s.
flashcards.example: If 60 cm³ of H₂ is produced in 30 seconds, average rate = 60 ÷ 30 = 2 cm³/s.

flashcards.definition: Draw a tangent line touching the curve at a specific time. Gradient of tangent = instantaneous rate at that time.
flashcards.example: A tangent at t=20s on a product vs time graph gives the rate at exactly that moment.

flashcards.definition: The reactant that is completely used up first, stopping the reaction. Determines the maximum amount of product.
flashcards.example: If Mg runs out before all the HCl reacts, Mg is the limiting reactant. The graph plateaus.

flashcards.definition: A protein catalyst that speeds up a specific biochemical reaction. Works at optimum temperature and pH.
flashcards.example: Catalase (in liver) rapidly decomposes H₂O₂ into water and oxygen.

flashcards.definition: Iron — catalyses N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. Without it, the reaction would be impractically slow even at high temperature.
flashcards.example: The Haber process produces ammonia for fertilisers that feed ~50% of the world's population.

flashcards.definition: Shows the spread of particle energies at a given temperature. Only particles with energy ≥ activation energy can react.
flashcards.example: Raising temperature shifts the curve right — a much larger proportion of particles exceed the activation energy.

questions.stem: According to collision theory, why does increasing temperature increase reaction rate?
choices: Particles get bigger
Particles move faster → more frequent collisions AND more collisions have energy ≥ activation energy
Temperature creates more particles
Activation energy decreases
questions.explanation: Higher temperature increases both collision frequency AND the proportion of particles exceeding the activation energy barrier.

questions.stem: Why does powdered marble react faster with acid than the same mass of large marble chips?
choices: Powder is chemically different
Greater surface area → more particles exposed to acid → more frequent collisions
Powder is hotter
Large chips are less pure
questions.explanation: Crushing increases surface area. More particles are available at the solid-liquid interface for collisions with acid particles.

questions.stem: A catalyst increases rate by:
choices: Increasing the energy of reactant particles
Providing an alternative pathway with lower activation energy
Being consumed and releasing energy
Increasing the concentration of reactants
questions.explanation: Catalysts lower the activation energy by offering an alternative mechanism. They are NOT consumed and do NOT change reactant energies.

questions.stem: On a product vs time graph, what does the plateau represent?
choices: The reaction is speeding up
The limiting reactant has been used up — the reaction is complete
The catalyst is exhausted
The temperature has dropped
questions.explanation: The plateau means no more product is being formed. The limiting reactant is completely consumed — the reaction has finished.

questions.stem: A reaction produces 48 cm³ of gas in 20 seconds. What is the average rate?
choices: 0.42 cm³/s
2.4 cm³/s
9.6 cm³/s
68 cm³/s
questions.explanation: Rate = amount ÷ time = 48 ÷ 20 = 2.4 cm³/s.

questions.stem: Two reactions use the same amounts of reactants but one is at 30°C, the other at 50°C. How will the graphs differ?
choices: The 50°C graph will be steeper initially but both reach the same final plateau
Both graphs will be identical
The 50°C graph will reach a higher plateau
The 30°C graph will be steeper
questions.explanation: Higher temperature → faster rate → steeper initial gradient. But same amount of limiting reactant → same final amount of product → same plateau height.

questions.stem: Which change will NOT increase the rate of a reaction between two solutions?
choices: Increase temperature
Increase concentration of one reactant
Add a catalyst
Increase the volume of the container (diluting both solutions)
questions.explanation: Increasing container volume without adding more reactant DILUTES the solution → lower concentration → slower rate. All other options increase rate.

questions.stem: Why does a catalyst NOT affect the amount of product formed?
choices: Catalysts are too weak
Catalysts only lower activation energy — they do NOT change the energies of reactants or products. ΔH and equilibrium position are unchanged
Catalysts stop working after a short time
Catalysts are always completely consumed
questions.explanation: Catalysts change the PATHWAY (lowering activation energy) but not the starting point (reactants) or end point (products). Therefore the yield is unchanged.

questions.stem: In the sodium thiosulfate + HCl reaction, why does the cross disappear faster at higher temperatures?
choices: The ink dissolves faster in warm solution
Higher temperature → faster reaction → sulfur precipitate forms more quickly → cross obscured sooner
The cross fades from the heat
HCl evaporates faster, concentrating the acid
questions.explanation: The sulfur precipitate (solid S) makes the solution cloudy. Higher temperature → faster rate → precipitate appears sooner → cross disappears in less time.

questions.stem: What does the steepness (gradient) of a product vs time curve tell you?
choices: The total amount of product
The rate of reaction — steeper gradient = faster rate
The activation energy
The temperature of the reaction
questions.explanation: Gradient = Δy/Δx = amount of product formed per unit time = rate. The initial gradient is the steepest because reactant concentrations are highest.

questions.stem: An enzyme-catalysed reaction stops working above 60°C. Why?
choices: The substrate runs out
The enzyme denatures — its active site loses shape → it can no longer bind the substrate → no catalysis
Enzymes evaporate at high temperatures
The activation energy becomes infinite
questions.explanation: Enzymes are proteins. High temperatures break the bonds maintaining their 3D shape (denaturation). The active site is deformed → substrate no longer fits → no catalysis.

questions.stem: Higher pressure increases the rate of gas-phase reactions because:
choices: Gas particles get larger
More particles in the same volume → more frequent collisions
Pressure heats up the gas
The activation energy decreases
questions.explanation: Increasing pressure compresses the gas → particles are closer together → higher concentration → more frequent collisions per unit time.

questions.stem: On a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, what effect does raising temperature have?
choices: The curve shifts left
The curve flattens and shifts right — more particles have higher energy, and a larger proportion exceed the activation energy
The activation energy line moves down
The curve becomes narrower
questions.explanation: Higher temperature flattens and shifts the distribution to the right. The key point: the area under the curve beyond the activation energy line increases dramatically.

questions.stem: Manganese(IV) oxide (MnO₂) catalyses H₂O₂ decomposition. After the reaction, the MnO₂:
choices: Is completely used up
Remains chemically unchanged — it can be filtered out and reused
Has become MnO
Has dissolved in the water produced
questions.explanation: Catalysts are NOT consumed. MnO₂ remains at the end — it can be recovered by filtration and used again for another batch of H₂O₂.

questions.stem: A student wants to find the rate at exactly t = 30 seconds from a curved product-time graph. They should:
choices: Read the y-value at t = 30s
Draw a tangent at t = 30s and calculate its gradient
Calculate the average rate over the whole reaction
Draw a straight line from (0,0) to the endpoint
questions.explanation: For instantaneous rate at a specific time, draw a tangent touching the curve at that point. The tangent's gradient = rate at that instant.

questions.stem: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes slowly at room temperature but much faster when warmed to 40°C. Using collision theory, the best explanation is:
choices: The heat makes the hydrogen peroxide molecules break apart on their own
The particles gain kinetic energy, so they collide more often and a greater proportion of collisions have enough energy to react
The heat lowers the activation energy of the reaction
Warming increases the concentration of the hydrogen peroxide
questions.explanation: Higher temperature gives particles more kinetic energy: collisions are more frequent AND more of them exceed the activation energy. Temperature does not change the activation energy or the concentration.

questions.stem: A whole antacid tablet fizzes slowly in water, but a crushed tablet fizzes much faster. Why?
choices: Crushing the tablet makes it more concentrated
Crushing exposes a larger surface area, so more particles can collide with the water each second
The crushed tablet is warmer than the whole tablet
Small pieces react faster because they contain a catalyst
questions.explanation: Breaking a solid into smaller pieces increases its surface area. More particles are available at the surface for collisions, so successful collisions happen more frequently and the rate rises.

questions.stem: Which statement about catalysts is correct?
choices: Catalysts are used up during the reaction
A catalyst increases the amount of product formed
A catalyst speeds up a reaction and is chemically unchanged at the end
Only enzymes can act as catalysts
questions.explanation: A catalyst provides a lower-activation-energy pathway and is not consumed — it is chemically unchanged when the reaction ends. It speeds up the reaction but does not change the yield.

questions.stem: A mass vs time graph for marble chips reacting with acid slopes downwards and then becomes horizontal. The horizontal section shows that:
choices: The reaction is still speeding up
The gas syringe is full
The reaction has finished — the limiting reactant is used up, so no more CO₂ escapes
The balance has stopped working
questions.explanation: The mass stops falling when no more carbon dioxide is being produced — the limiting reactant has been completely consumed and the reaction is complete.

questions.stem: In a mass-loss experiment, the mass falls by 1.2 g in 40 seconds. What is the average rate of mass loss?
choices: 33 g/s
48 g/s
questions.explanation: Rate = change in mass ÷ time = 1.2 ÷ 40 = 0.03 g/s. Dividing time by mass (40 ÷ 1.2 ≈ 33) inverts the calculation.

questions.stem: A student reacts 1 g of powdered calcium carbonate with excess hydrochloric acid, then repeats with 1 g of large marble chips in the same excess acid. How do the two product vs time graphs compare?
choices: The powder graph is steeper at first and reaches a higher plateau
The chips graph is steeper because larger pieces react more
The powder graph is steeper initially, but both level off at the same final amount of product
Both graphs are identical because the same mass is used
questions.explanation: Powder has a greater surface area, so it reacts faster (steeper initial gradient). But both samples contain the same mass of CaCO₃ and the acid is in excess, so both produce the same total amount of product — the same plateau.

questions.stem: Which change will increase the rate of reaction between magnesium ribbon and dilute hydrochloric acid?
choices: Use a more concentrated acid
Use a larger beaker
Dilute the acid with water
Cool the acid in an ice bath
questions.explanation: A more concentrated acid has more particles per unit volume → more frequent collisions → faster rate. Cooling slows the reaction, diluting lowers the concentration, and a larger beaker changes nothing about the reactants.

questions.stem: On an energy profile diagram, how does adding a catalyst change the diagram?
choices: The activation energy hump is lower, but the energy difference between reactants and products stays the same
The products move to a lower energy level
The activation energy hump is higher
Both the reactants and the products move to higher energy levels
questions.explanation: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy — only the hump shrinks. The energies of reactants and products (and therefore ΔH) are unchanged, so the yield is unchanged too.

questions.stem: In the sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid experiment, a student times how long a cross under the flask takes to disappear. What causes the cross to disappear?
choices: The acid dissolves the ink in the cross
The solution boils and the steam hides the cross
A precipitate of sulfur forms, making the mixture cloudy enough to hide the cross
The sodium thiosulfate turns black
questions.explanation: The reaction produces solid sulfur as a fine precipitate. As more sulfur forms, the mixture becomes increasingly cloudy until the cross can no longer be seen through it.

questions.stem: On a graph of gas volume collected against time, what does a steeper curve show?
choices: A faster reaction — more gas is being produced each second
A larger total amount of gas
A higher temperature
A longer reaction time
questions.explanation: Gradient = change in volume ÷ change in time = rate of gas production. A steeper gradient means gas is being produced more quickly — a faster reaction.

questions.stem: An enzyme-catalysed reaction is very slow at 5°C but speeds up again when warmed to 37°C. This shows that at 5°C:
choices: The enzyme has been denatured
The enzyme has been killed
The substrate has frozen
The enzyme is intact but less active — particles move slowly at low temperature, so enzyme-substrate collisions are rare
questions.explanation: Low temperature slows the reaction because particles have less kinetic energy and collide less often. The enzyme is NOT denatured — denaturation permanently destroys the active site, and warming would not restore the activity.

questions.stem: The Haber process is run at high pressure. In terms of collision theory, this increases the rate because:
choices: The high pressure lowers the activation energy
The high pressure gives each particle more energy
Compressing the gases pushes the particles closer together, so collisions happen more frequently
The high pressure turns the gases into liquids
questions.explanation: Higher pressure squeezes the same number of gas particles into a smaller volume — effectively a higher concentration — so collisions between reactant particles are more frequent. It does not change the activation energy or the particles' energy.

questions.stem: On a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve, what changes when a catalyst is added?
choices: The curve shifts to higher energies
The curve becomes taller and narrower
The activation energy line moves to the left, so a larger proportion of particles now have enough energy to react
The total number of particles increases
questions.explanation: A catalyst lowers the activation energy, so on the distribution the Ea line moves left: more particles have energy ≥ Ea and can react. The curve itself does not move — the particles' energies only change with temperature.
